Since inception, Tenk Investment Limited has earned an estimated 18.9%, net of fees and expenses.2 Market Update We have long argued that the 2-Year Treasury Yield will tell you what the Federal Reserve will do before the Fed actually moves; during the 3rd quarter, the 2-year UST rose by ~75 basis points.3 Once again, this adage proved correct as the FOMC hiked interest rates for the first time since July 2023 by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00% in September. Unfortunately, as the US/Iran ceasefire unraveled, oil returned to triple digits, and the ten-year Treasury yield posted its largest quarterly increase since 1994. Despite these conditions, Investment Grade credit spreads finished the quarter at ~85 basis points, the S&P 500 set a record high in August, and the VIX touched its low for the year in mid-August (interestingly small-cap equities fell ~7%!). In short, it was a quarter of higher rates, higher energy prices and calm risk markets … until the final six trading days of September, when high yield spreads widened ~40 basis points!

blocks.html: Credit spreads were calm for most of the quarter until they weren’t! Although Investment Grade spreads only drifted from ~75 basis points at the end of June to ~85 basis points at the end of September, high yield spreads tightened to ~260 basis points at the end of August before widening ~52 basis points into quarter-end to ~312 basis points (~40 basis points of that move coming in the final six trading days of the quarter as the Treasury selloff accelerated).4 Despite the widening, the 20-year average for HY remains ~488 basis points, so even after the September widening, spreads do not indicate stress. The message from the public credit markets appears to be that higher rates, rather than credit deterioration, are the current story.

blocks.html: Many describe the labor market as “low hire, low fire”: initial jobless claims have fallen to their lowest levels in more than two years even as hiring has stalled, and average hourly earnings growth has slowed to 3.0% year over year, the lowest since 2021.12 We think this adage is more applicable for “white collar” work than for “blue collar” work given the shortage of qualified labor. To that end, construction and manufacturing payrolls were both positive in September, and small businesses continue to cite the availability of qualified labor — not a lack of demand for it — as their single biggest problem.13

The aforementioned moves in energy kept headline CPI at 3.4%–3.5% year over year through August, and the September report, released on October 14th, came in hotter still at 3.7%, with gasoline up ~34% year over year.14 However, core inflation was cooler as the core CPI eased from 2.9% in May to 2.4% in August before ticking back up to 2.6% in September; core PCE — the Fed’s preferred measure — printed 3.0% in August, with the BEA’s annual revision on September 30th marking down June and July to 3.0% from the 3.3% originally reported.15

blocks.html: In short, company commentary is consistent with what BasePoint continues to observe: average Main Street consumers and small businesses are holding up, with gasoline rather than tariffs now the primary squeeze on discretionary budgets. Blue-collar employment availability remains the single most important variable for the health of the consumer portfolios we finance, and on that front the data remain constructive: employers are holding onto workers, initial claims are at multi- year lows, and small businesses continue to report more openings than qualified applicants. BasePoint’s borrowers continue to exhibit stable credit performance. Daily data files provide continuous visibility into underlying portfolio health, and we are not seeing material credit degradation or heightened delinquencies across our borrowers.21

blocks.html: Vintage analysis is the foundation of how BasePoint underwrites. In a portfolio of consumer or small business receivables, a vintage is a cohort of loans originated in a given period; we have tremendous amounts of data on how those cohorts pay down, how losses emerge, and how the curve shifts through various economic scenarios. blocks.html: There is no through-cycle vintage curve to point to when thinking about underwriting. The asset class is roughly three years old and has never experienced a demand downturn. We underwrite from loss curves with realized history, not from a short- term pricing curve that fell by a third to a half despite a boom! For us to participate here, just as is the case in the consumer loan market and the small business receivable market, amortization would need to match contracted cashflow (i.e. a facility that fully amortizes within the term of the offtake contract and does not rely on re-leasing or residual value). We think the right way to lend here is via vintage-specific borrowing bases where advance rates are set by chip generation and reset against observable rental indices, the way we true up a receivables borrowing base weekly. If a lender is going to own the technology tail, it should be paid equity-like returns for it, not a spread.

blocks.html: The Fund’s exposure breakdown shows positions beyond traditional asset-based lending. We view each of these positions as supported, directly or indirectly, by the same underlying assets: the receivables generated by the originators that BasePoint finances. The traditional asset-based facilities in which the Fund participates are structured and monitored by BasePoint against a borrowing base. Where the Fund holds corporate exposure to an originator, that financing is typically extended to fund growth of the originator’s receivables portfolio, and in most cases the cash flow from those receivables is the primary source of repayment. The Fund’s equity exposure consists of preferred equity or warrants that BasePoint, in providing flexible capital to its originators, negotiates from time to time and in which the Fund may participate. These positions are typically participating preferred or similar instruments that generate current income rather than common equity held for appreciation. The Fund does not pursue a standalone equity strategy; the equity positions are incidental to the Fund’s lending, and the Fund’s returns are intended to be driven primarily by the short duration and cash generation of the underlying receivables. We believe one of BasePoint’s differentiating aspects as a lender is its ability to offer bespoke capital solutions to its originators as their businesses grow and their capital needs change. We seek to structure investments such that the principal driver of the Fund’s credit risk remains the cash generation of the underlying receivables.
